docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome to the McCreary family heritage site. The goal of this site is to store resources related to educating people about the McCreary family history and their migration from Scotland, and Ireland to locations around the world. We don't simply store genealogical data. We also use web-based tools to alow students to explore this information.

Please see the About page for more details about this site.

Please contact me on LinkedIn if you have any comments, feedback or suggestions on how we can improve the site.

  • Dan McCreary, October 2025

docs.title: How We Built This Site
docs.text: This page describes how we built this website and some of the rationale behind why we made various design choices.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: MicroSims are about how we use generative AI to create animations and simulations. The language of AI is Python. So we wanted to create a site that could be easily understood by Python developers.

docs.title: Mkdocs vs. Docusaurus
docs.text: There are two main tools used by Python developers to write documentation: Mkdocs and Docusaurus. Mkdocs is easier to use and more popular than Docusaurus. Docusaurus is also optimized for single-page applications. Mkdocs also has an extensive library of themes and plugins. None of us are experts in JavaScript or React. Based on our ChatGPT Analysis of the Tradeoffs we chose mkdocs for this site management.

docs.title: GitHub and GitHub Pages
docs.text:
GitHub is a logical choice to store our site source code and documentation. GitHub also has a Custom GitHub Action that does auto-deployment if any files on the site change. We don't currently have this action enabled, but other teams can use this feature if they don't have the ability to do a local build with mkdocs.

GitHub also has Issues, Projects and releases that we can use to manage our bugs and tasks.

The best practice for low-cost websites that have public-only content is GitHub Pages. Mkdocs has a command (mkdocs gh-deploy) that does deployment directly to GitHub Pages. This was an easy choice to make.

docs.title: GitHub Clone
docs.text:
If you would like to clone this repository, here are the commands:

mkdir projects
cd projects
git clone https://github.com/dmccreary/microsims

docs.title: After Changes
docs.text:
After you make local changes you must do the following:

# add the new files to a a local commit transaction
git add FILES
# Execute the a local commit with a message about what and why you are doing the commit
git commit -m "comment"
# Update the central GitHub repository
git push

docs.title: Material Theme
docs.text:
We had several options when picking a mkdocs theme:

  1. Mkdocs default
  2. Readthedocs
  3. Third-Party Themes See Ranking

The Material Theme had 16K stars. No other theme had over a few hundred. This was also an easy design decision.

One key criterial was the social Open Graph tags so that when our users post a link to a simulation, the image of the simulation is included in the link. Since Material supported this, we used the Material theme. You can see our ChatGPT Design Decision Analysis if you want to check our decision process.

docs.title: Enable Edit Icon
docs.text:
To enable the Edit icon on all pages, you must add the edit_uri and the content.action.edit under the theme features area.

edit_uri: edit/master/docs/

    theme:
        features:
            - content.action.edit

docs.title: Conda vs VENV
docs.text:
There are two choices for virtual environments. We can use the native Python venv or use Conda. venv is simle but is only designed for pure Python projects. We imagine that this site could use JavaScript and other langauges in the future, so we picked Conda. There is nothing on this microsite that prevents you from using one or the other. See the ChatGPT Analysis Here.

Here is the conda script that we ran to create a new mkdocs environment that also supports the material social imaging libraries.

conda deactivate
conda create -n mkdocs python=3
conda activate mkdocs
pip install mkdocs "mkdocs-material[imaging]"

docs.title: Mkdocs Commands
docs.text: There are three simple mkdoc commands we use.

docs.title: Local Build
docs.text:
mkdocs build

This builds your website in a folder called site. Use this to test that the mkdocs.yml site is working and does not have any errors.

docs.title: Run a Local Server
docs.text:
mkdocs serve

This runs a server on http://localhost:8000. Use this to test the display formatting locally before you push your code up to the GitHub repo.

mkdoc gh-deploy

This pushes everything up to the GitHub Pages site. Note that it does not commit your code to GitHub.

docs.title: Mkdocs Material Social Tags
docs.text:
We are using the Material Social tags. This is a work in progress!

Here is what we have learned.

  1. There are extensive image processing libraries that can't be installed with just pip. You will need to run a tool like brew on the Mac to get the libraries installed.
  2. Even after brew installs the libraries, you have to get your environment to find the libraries. The only way I could get that to work was to set up a local UNIX environment variable.

Here is the brew command that I ran:

brew install cairo freetype libffi libjpeg libpng zlib

I then had to add the following to my ~/.zshrc file:

export DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/homebrew/lib

Note that I am running on a Mac with Apple silicon. This means that the image libraries that brew downloads must be specific to the Mac Arm instruction set.

  • Cover images for blog post #4364
  • Discussion on overriding the Social Card Image

docs.title: Introduction to McCreary Heritage
docs.text:
Welcome to the story of the McCreary family—a story that spans centuries and continents, from the rugged highlands of Scotland to the green hills of Ireland, and finally across the Atlantic Ocean to North America. This is more than just a collection of names and dates. It's the story of real people who faced hardships, made difficult choices, and built new lives in unfamiliar lands.

If you're reading this, you might be researching your own family history, completing a school project, or simply curious about how ordinary people lived through extraordinary times. Whatever brought you here, you'll discover that the McCreary family's journey is deeply connected to major historical events that shaped the modern world.

docs.title: Who Were the McCrearys?
docs.text:
The McCreary surname has its roots in Scotland, though you might see it spelled in different ways: MacCreary, McCreery, McCrory, MacRory, or even Magrory. In Scottish Gaelic, the name Mac Ruairidh means "son of Rory," with Rory itself meaning "red king." Like many Scottish surnames, it identifies a family's ancestral line and connects them to a particular clan or region.

The McCrearys were part of Scotland's complex clan system, where extended families lived together, shared resources, and defended common territory. Understanding where your ancestors came from—and why they left—requires looking beyond individual family trees to see the bigger picture of Scottish and Irish history.

[Suggested Image: Map showing Scotland, Ireland (with Ulster highlighted), and eastern North America, with arrows indicating migration routes]

docs.title: The Three-Part Journey
docs.text: The McCreary story unfolds in three distinct chapters, each shaped by the politics, economics, and religious conflicts of its time:

docs.title: 1. Scotland: The Homeland (Before 1600s)
docs.text: The McCreary families originated in Scotland, particularly in the western regions and islands. Scotland in the 1500s and early 1600s was a place of both beauty and hardship. Families farmed small plots of land, raised livestock, and lived in tight-knit communities. However, Scotland was also experiencing significant upheaval. Religious conflicts between Catholics and Protestants created tension, while English political pressure threatened Scottish independence. For many Scottish families, economic opportunity was limited, and life was becoming increasingly difficult.

docs.title: 2. Ireland: The Ulster Plantation (1600s-1700s)
docs.text:
Beginning in the early 1600s, the British government implemented a plan called the Ulster Plantation—a organized settlement scheme designed to establish Protestant communities in northern Ireland (Ulster). Thousands of Scottish families, including many McCrearys, were offered land and incentives to relocate across the narrow sea to Ireland.

This migration wasn't simply about seeking better farmland. It was part of a larger political strategy to control Ireland by transplanting loyal Protestant settlers into a predominantly Catholic region. The Scottish settlers who accepted this opportunity—who would become known as the Scotch-Irish or Ulster Scots—found themselves in a complicated position. They were newcomers in a land where they weren't entirely welcome, caught between their Scottish heritage and their new Irish home.

[Suggested Image: Illustration or period map of the Ulster Plantation showing townlands and settlements]

docs.title: 3. North America: The Great Migration (1700s-1800s)
docs.text:
By the early 1700s, life in Ulster had become difficult for many Scotch-Irish families. They faced high rents imposed by English landlords, restrictions on their Presbyterian religious practices, and limited economic opportunities. When they heard about available land in the American colonies, many McCreary families made the momentous decision to cross the Atlantic Ocean—a dangerous journey that typically took six to eight weeks.

In North America, McCreary families primarily settled in Pennsylvania, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and later pushed westward into Tennessee, Kentucky, and beyond. They brought with them their Presbyterian faith, their farming skills, their traditions, and their fierce independence. These qualities would help shape the character of the American frontier.

docs.title: Why This History Matters
docs.text:
You might wonder why we should care about events that happened centuries ago. Here are several reasons why McCreary family heritage remains relevant today:

Understanding Identity: If you have McCreary ancestors, their experiences are part of your own family story. Knowing where you came from helps you understand who you are.

Historical Connections: The McCreary family's journey touches on major historical themes—religious conflict, colonialism, immigration, and the settlement of the American frontier. Their personal stories make these abstract historical concepts real and relatable.

Cultural Heritage: The Scotch-Irish brought distinctive traditions in music, language, food, and community life that still influence American culture today, particularly in Appalachia and the American South.

Research Skills: Tracing family history teaches valuable research skills—how to evaluate sources, verify information, and piece together evidence to solve historical mysteries.

Human Resilience: Perhaps most importantly, these stories remind us of human courage and adaptability. The McCrearys and families like them faced uncertain futures, left everything familiar behind, and built new lives from scratch—not once, but multiple times.

[Suggested Image: Three-panel comparison showing traditional Scottish, Ulster Irish, and American frontier settlements]

docs.title: What You'll Find on This Site
docs.text:
This website is organized to help you explore McCreary heritage from multiple angles:

If you're researching your family tree, you'll find documented family lines, genealogical resources, and tips for connecting to McCreary ancestry. The Family History & Genealogy section provides the tools you need to trace your own connections.

If you're studying history, you'll discover how the McCreary story fits into broader historical movements. The Historical Timeline & Context section connects family history to major events like the Protestant Reformation, the Ulster Plantation, and American westward expansion.

If you're interested in geography, interactive maps show migration patterns and settlement locations. The Geography & Settlement Patterns section explains why families chose particular locations and how the physical landscape shaped their lives.

If you're planning a heritage trip, the Heritage Tourism Guide provides practical information for visiting McCreary-related sites in Scotland and Ireland today.

If you're a teacher or student, the Educational Resources section offers lesson plans, primary sources, and materials designed specifically for classroom use.

Throughout the site, you'll find personal stories that bring history to life—letters, diaries, biographies, and accounts that show how individual McCreary family members experienced the major events of their times.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text:
Everyone comes to family history with different interests and different levels of experience. Here are some suggestions for getting started:

  • Use the search function to look for specific names, places, or topics
  • Follow the chronological path through the Historical Timeline to see how events unfolded
  • Explore the maps in the Geography section to visualize migration patterns
  • Read individual stories in the Stories & Biographies section to connect with personal experiences
  • Check the Glossary whenever you encounter unfamiliar terms
  • Consult the Resources section for links to archives, databases, and other research tools

Remember, this is an ongoing research project. Family history is never truly complete—there are always new discoveries to be made, new connections to establish, and new stories to uncover. If you have information to contribute or questions to ask, please use the Contact page to get in touch.

[Suggested Chart: Timeline showing major events in McCreary family history from 1500-1900, with parallel tracks for Scotland, Ireland, and North America]

docs.title: Beginning the Journey
docs.text:
The McCreary family story is ultimately about movement—physical movement across oceans and borders, but also social movement as families adapted to new circumstances and built new communities. It's about the push and pull of history: being pushed out by religious persecution and economic hardship, pulled forward by the promise of land and opportunity.

As you explore this site, try to imagine the real people behind the historical facts. Picture a Scottish farmer deciding whether to accept land in Ulster. Envision a family boarding a ship for America, not knowing if they would survive the voyage. Consider what it meant to carve a farm from wilderness, to build a church in a new settlement, to maintain old traditions while adapting to new realities.

Their choices created possibilities for future generations—possibly including you. Their story is worth knowing, worth preserving, and worth passing on.

Let's begin.

Next: About This Site | Family History & Genealogy

docs.title: Family History and Genealogy
docs.text: This section serves the largest expected audience - family genealogists. Include documented family lines, surname spelling variations, major family branches, genealogical resources, DNA research guidance, and tips for connecting to McCreary ancestry. Feature downloadable family trees, links to relevant archives, and guidance on breaking through research brick walls.

docs.title: Historical Timeline & Context
docs.text: A chronological journey through McCreary family history set against major historical events. Cover life in Scotland, the Ulster Plantation in Ireland, religious and political conflicts, and the Great Migration to North America. This serves both educators and students with clear, dated milestones and connections to broader historical movements.

docs.title: Geography & Settlement Patterns
docs.text:
Interactive and static maps showing where McCreary families originated in Scotland, settled in Ireland (particularly Ulster), and migrated to in North America. Include information about the landscape, climate, and physical environment of these regions. Feature before-and-after comparisons and explanations of why certain locations were chosen. This serves geographic researchers, heritage tourists, and genealogists trying to locate ancestral lands.

*

docs.title: Educational Resources
docs.text:
Materials specifically designed for teachers and students with support for a wide audience of age ranges from grade school to advanced genealogy researchers.

Include lesson plans, primary source documents with analysis guides, discussion questions, timelines suitable for classroom use, and connections to curriculum standards. Offer downloadable materials and suggestions for student projects. Feature age-appropriate content summaries and citation guidance.

docs.title: Heritage Tourism Guide
docs.text: Practical information for visiting McCreary-related sites in Scotland and Ireland. Include specific locations (churches, graveyards, townlands, estates), travel tips, recommended itineraries, local heritage centers and museums, and guidance on accessing local records. Provide photographs of sites as they appear today alongside historical context.

docs.title: Culture & Traditions**
docs.text: Explore Scotch-Irish cultural heritage through the McCreary family lens. Cover language, music, foodways, religious practices (particularly Presbyterian traditions), crafts, folklore, and how these traditions evolved as families migrated. Include stories that illustrate daily life, celebrations, and community practices.

docs.title: Research & Scholarship**
docs.text: Academic resources including bibliographies, primary source locations and archives, methodological notes on genealogical verification, historiographical context, opportunities for collaboration, and invitations to contribute research. This serves academic researchers and serious local historians with the rigor they require.

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
Stories & Biographies

Individual narratives that bring history to life. Feature profiles of notable McCreary family members, ordinary people whose lives illustrate historical themes, first-person accounts, letters and diaries, and oral histories. These human stories engage all personas but are particularly valuable for educators looking for compelling classroom material.

docs.title: Generating McCreary Family Heritage Website Personas
Sample Prompt
docs.text:
Prompt

Personas for the McCreary family heritage website:

I want to build a new website about the McCreary family heritage. Our focus is the Scotch-Irish people with the Surname "McCreary" and its related spellings.

This focus of the website is education about the McCreary family heritage and its role in the history of Scotland, Ireland and migration to new locations in North America. I want the site to be useful as a resource for schools teaching the history of Scotland, Ireland as well and people that are doing research into their Scottish and Irish background.

Please help me describe the personas of people that might be using this website. Include history students, teachers, people doing historical research, and people doing research into their own personal genealogy. Include people that might want to travel to Scotland and Ireland and visit the areas where the McCreary family lived. Include people interested in the geography of the land and the climate of the area where the McCreary family originated.

For each persona, create a persona name in a level-3 heading and then describe the persona in detail in the body text. Then create a detailed list of questions they might have and the types of information they are looking for.

List the personas in the frequency order you predict they will arrive at the site. This information can then be used to help organize the site top-level navigation.

docs.title: Family Genealogist
docs.text:
The Family Genealogist is someone researching their personal ancestry who has discovered or suspects a connection to the McCreary surname. They range from beginners just starting their family tree to experienced researchers with decades of genealogical work. They may have found the McCreary name in census records, birth certificates, immigration documents, or family stories passed down through generations. These researchers are often emotionally invested in their search, seeking to understand their identity and connect with their roots.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What are the variant spellings of McCreary (McCrary, McCreery, MacCrory, etc.) and how do I know which spelling my ancestors used?
  • Where in Scotland and Ireland did McCreary families primarily live?
  • When did major waves of McCreary migration to North America occur?
  • Are there documented McCreary family lines with published genealogies I can connect to?
  • What records are available for researching McCreary ancestors (church records, land grants, immigration lists)?
  • How can I break through brick walls in my McCreary research?
  • Are there DNA testing strategies specific to identifying McCreary connections?
  • What McCreary family associations or societies exist that I can join?
  • Where can I find photographs or descriptions of ancestral McCreary properties?
  • What occupations were common among McCreary families historically?

docs.title: History Educator
docs.text:
The History Educator is a middle school, high school, or college instructor teaching courses on Scottish history, Irish history, immigration history, or Scotch-Irish culture. They are looking for engaging, well-sourced materials to supplement their curriculum and make history come alive for students. They value primary sources, visual materials, and narratives that illustrate broader historical themes through specific family examples. They need content that is academically credible while being accessible to their students' reading levels.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • How does the McCreary family story illustrate larger patterns of Scotch-Irish migration?
  • What primary source documents are available that students can analyze?
  • How did the McCreary family experience major historical events (Ulster Plantation, Scottish Lowland conflicts, American frontier settlement)?
  • What teaching resources (lesson plans, worksheets, timelines) are available?
  • How can I use the McCreary story to teach about push-pull factors in migration?
  • What maps show McCreary settlement patterns in Scotland, Ireland, and North America?
  • Are there stories of individual McCreary family members that would engage students?
  • How does McCreary history connect to curriculum standards for Scottish, Irish, or American history?
  • What visual materials (photographs, illustrations, artifacts) can I use in presentations?
  • How can I cite this website as a credible source in academic contexts?

docs.title: Academic Researcher
docs.text:
The Academic Researcher is a graduate student, professor, or independent scholar studying Scotch-Irish history, migration patterns, Scottish clans, Ulster settlement, or related topics. They may be writing papers, theses, dissertations, or books that touch on themes illustrated by the McCreary family experience. They require rigorous documentation, original sources, and scholarly analysis. They are interested in how the McCreary family story contributes to broader historiographical debates and may be looking for gaps in the existing research.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What primary sources document McCreary family history and where are they archived?
  • How does McCreary family history contribute to understanding Scotch-Irish identity formation?
  • What scholarly works have already been published about the McCreary family or related clans?
  • Are there unexplored archives or collections relevant to McCreary research?
  • How do McCreary migration patterns compare to other Scotch-Irish families?
  • What economic, religious, and political factors influenced McCreary movements?
  • Are there statistical data on McCreary population distributions over time?
  • What methodology has been used to verify McCreary family connections?
  • Can I access bibliographies or finding aids for McCreary-related research?
  • Are there opportunities to contribute to or collaborate on McCreary historical projects?

docs.title: Heritage Tourist
docs.text:
The Heritage Tourist is someone planning to visit Scotland and Ireland, either because they have McCreary ancestry or because they are interested in Scotch-Irish heritage more broadly. They want to walk the land their ancestors walked, visit churches where they worshipped, see the landscapes they farmed, and experience the culture that shaped them. They are planning a trip and need practical information about locations to visit, but they also want historical context to make their visit meaningful.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What specific locations in Scotland and Ireland are associated with McCreary families?
  • Can I visit ancestral McCreary homes, farms, or estates?
  • What churches, graveyards, or monuments have McCreary connections?
  • What towns or regions should I include in my heritage tour itinerary?
  • Are there guided tours focused on Scotch-Irish heritage or McCreary history?
  • What museums or heritage centers interpret the Scotch-Irish experience?
  • What is the best time of year to visit these locations?
  • How do I access local records or historical societies in Scotland and Ireland?
  • What modern amenities exist near historical McCreary sites?
  • Are there festivals or cultural events celebrating Scotch-Irish heritage I could attend?

docs.title: History Student
docs.text:
The History Student is typically in high school or college, working on an assignment related to Scottish history, Irish history, immigration, or cultural studies. They may have been assigned to research a specific surname, trace a migration pattern, or write about Scotch-Irish contributions to American history. They need clear, organized information that helps them complete their assignment efficiently while also being engaging enough to hold their interest. They value summaries, timelines, and resources that help them get started quickly.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What is the origin and meaning of the McCreary surname?
  • What is a brief overview of McCreary family history I can use for my assignment?
  • What are the most important dates and events in McCreary family history?
  • How do I cite information from this website for my paper or project?
  • What are good starting points for learning about the Scotch-Irish?
  • Can I find quotes or stories that would work well in my presentation?
  • What maps or charts can I use to illustrate McCreary migration?
  • How does the McCreary story connect to what we're studying in class?
  • Are there videos or interactive elements that explain the history?
  • Where can I find additional sources if I need to go deeper?

docs.title: Local Historian
docs.text:
The Local Historian is someone researching the history of a specific town, county, or region in Scotland, Ireland, or North America where McCreary families settled. They may be writing a local history book, creating a museum exhibit, maintaining a historical society website, or simply preserving community heritage. They are interested in how the McCreary family fits into the larger story of their area and may have access to local records or oral histories that could contribute to the broader McCreary narrative.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • Which McCreary families lived in my specific area and when?
  • How did McCreary families contribute to local economic, political, or religious life?
  • Are there McCreary-built structures still standing in my area?
  • What local records mention McCreary families?
  • How do McCreary families connect to other prominent local families?
  • Are there local stories, legends, or traditions associated with McCreary families?
  • What land did McCreary families own in my area?
  • How can I contribute local McCreary information to this website?
  • Are there photographs of local McCreary individuals or properties?
  • What role did McCreary families play in local conflicts or notable events?

docs.title: Cultural Enthusiast
docs.text:
The Cultural Enthusiast is interested in Scotch-Irish culture, traditions, music, language, foodways, and customs. They may not have McCreary ancestry themselves, but they appreciate the broader cultural heritage and want to understand how families like the McCrearys preserved and adapted their cultural traditions over time and across geography. They might be involved in Celtic cultural organizations, traditional music groups, or heritage festivals.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What cultural traditions did McCreary families maintain from Scotland and Ireland?
  • What language (Scots, Irish, English dialects) did McCreary families speak?
  • What music and songs were part of McCreary family culture?
  • What foods and recipes were traditional in McCreary households?
  • How did McCreary families celebrate holidays and life events?
  • What crafts or skills were passed down through McCreary generations?
  • How did McCreary family culture change in the New World?
  • What Presbyterian or religious traditions were important to McCreary families?
  • Are there examples of McCreary family folklore or storytelling traditions?
  • How does McCreary culture compare to other Scotch-Irish families?

docs.title: Geographic Researcher
docs.text:
The Geographic Researcher is interested in the physical landscape, climate, and environmental context of the regions where McCreary families lived. They may be geographers, environmental historians, agricultural historians, or simply people fascinated by how landscape shapes culture and history. They want to understand the terrain, climate, natural resources, and geographic challenges that influenced where McCreary families settled and how they lived.

Key Questions and Information Needs:

  • What is the topography and physical geography of original McCreary territories in Scotland?
  • What was the climate like in the areas where McCreary families originated?
  • What natural resources were available in these regions?
  • How did geography influence McCreary settlement patterns?
  • What were the agricultural capabilities of lands where McCreary families farmed?
  • How does the geography of McCreary settlements in North America compare to Scotland and Ireland?
  • What role did rivers, mountains, and coastlines play in McCreary family history?
  • How has the landscape changed since McCreary families lived there?
  • What were the ecological challenges McCreary families faced?
  • Are there historical maps showing McCreary lands in their geographic context?

docs.title: Generating a README.md file

docs.title: Suggested Website Layout for McCreary Family Heritage
docs.text: Based on the personas identified, here is a recommended structure that organizes content to serve the most frequent visitors while remaining accessible to all users:

docs.title: Primary Navigation Structure
docs.text:
Home

About This Site

Introduction to McCreary Heritage

An overview of the Scotch-Irish McCreary families, the surname origins and variations, and what visitors can expect to learn from the site.

Family History & Genealogy

This section serves the largest expected audience - family genealogists. Include documented family lines, surname spelling variations, major family branches, genealogical resources, DNA research guidance, and tips for connecting to McCreary ancestry. Feature downloadable family trees, links to relevant archives, and guidance on breaking through research brick walls.

Historical Timeline & Context

A chronological journey through McCreary family history set against major historical events. Cover life in Scotland, the Ulster Plantation in Ireland, religious and political conflicts, and the Great Migration to North America. This serves both educators and students with clear, dated milestones and connections to broader historical movements.

Geography & Settlement Patterns

Interactive and static maps showing where McCreary families originated in Scotland, settled in Ireland (particularly Ulster), and migrated to in North America. Include information about the landscape, climate, and physical environment of these regions. Feature before-and-after comparisons and explanations of why certain locations were chosen. This serves geographic researchers, heritage tourists, and genealogists trying to locate ancestral lands.

Heritage Tourism Guide

Practical information for visiting McCreary-related sites in Scotland and Ireland. Include specific locations (churches, graveyards, townlands, estates), travel tips, recommended itineraries, local heritage centers and museums, and guidance on accessing local records. Provide photographs of sites as they appear today alongside historical context.

Educational Resources

Materials specifically designed for teachers and students. Include lesson plans, primary source documents with analysis guides, discussion questions, timelines suitable for classroom use, and connections to curriculum standards. Offer downloadable materials and suggestions for student projects. Feature age-appropriate content summaries and citation guidance.

Culture & Traditions

Explore Scotch-Irish cultural heritage through the McCreary family lens. Cover language, music, foodways, religious practices (particularly Presbyterian traditions), crafts, folklore, and how these traditions evolved as families migrated. Include stories that illustrate daily life, celebrations, and community practices.

Research & Scholarship

Academic resources including bibliographies, primary source locations and archives, methodological notes on genealogical verification, historiographical context, opportunities for collaboration, and invitations to contribute research. This serves academic researchers and serious local historians with the rigor they require.

Stories & Biographies

Individual narratives that bring history to life. Feature profiles of notable McCreary family members, ordinary people whose lives illustrate historical themes, first-person accounts, letters and diaries, and oral histories. These human stories engage all personas but are particularly valuable for educators looking for compelling classroom material.

Glossary

Resources

Comprehensive list of external resources including archives, libraries, genealogical databases, historical societies, relevant books and articles, DNA testing services, and related websites.

Contact

docs.title: Navigation Recommendations
docs.text:
Consider organizing the main navigation menu to prioritize the most frequently accessed sections:

  • Place "Family History & Genealogy" prominently in the navigation since genealogists are expected to be the largest visitor group
  • Make "Educational Resources" easily discoverable with clear labeling for teachers and students
  • Use descriptive menu labels that clearly indicate what each section contains
  • Consider a prominent search function since visitors will have diverse, specific needs
  • Include visual cues or icons to help visitors quickly identify relevant sections
  • Provide multiple pathways to content (chronological, geographical, topical) to accommodate different research approaches

This structure balances the needs of casual learners, serious researchers, and everyone in between while maintaining a logical flow that tells the comprehensive story of McCreary family heritage.
